newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Partial refunds fail to quell anger in Albania.
newsitem.headline: Partial refunds fail to quell anger in Albania.

text.p: Confusion, anger and resignation filled the grimy streets of Tirana on Tuesday as the government started to hand over partial refunds to investors caught out in a massive pyramid savings scandal.

"We have nothing to eat, no food, nothing," said Sofia Stadafa, a pensioner queuing outside a small bank booth in the centre of Albania's run-down capital. "Of course I want the money, but this is a big swindle."
Banks were told to start giving depositors from one failed pyramid scheme 60 percent of their cash on Tuesday in the first compensation programme organised by the ruling Democrats.
But only a few people turned up in bright winter sunshine at the nine designated booths when the time came for the refunds to arrive. Many investors demanded all their money back or nothing.

"I put $40,000 into this fund and want $40,000 back, not $24,000," said Stavrula Shehu, a young woman who invested all the money sent to her by relatives abroad. "If I accept their 60 percent, I can't hope for any more."

Many people who did want to claim a refund faced disappointment, with staff behind grills in the mobile offices under strict instructions on who to pay, depending on what day the money had been invested and where.
One of the booths pinned a list of just 21 eligible investors on its window, another had a list of 36. Nearly 150,000 people are believed to have put money in the pyramid scheme concerned.

"All I can say is that I want to start planting some bombs," said one frail elderly man, clutching a sheath of faded yellow receipts, as he was told to come back later in the week for his refund. "You are all thieves," he muttered.
Rumours have swirled through Tirana for days that the rightist government is keeping hold of cash from collapsed pyramid schemes.

Economists believe more than $1 billion is tied up in a swathe of such schemes across the country. Five leading funds have caved in and the government has so far frozen some $300 million from just two of the failed firms.
"They used our money to pay for their election campaigns," Shehu said, not frightened to speak her mind in front of a group of policemen standing guard by one of the booths.

Others in the crowd warned that if all the money was not returned, riots would break out across the small Balkan state. Nationwide disturbances shook the country last month, sparking a tough police crackdown.
"God knows what our future is. Imagine a people who are at the bottom of the ladder and have nothing to lose. Just see what we can do," one old man shouted.
A uniformed policeman queuing for his refund sympathised with the crowd of angry investors.
"If I'd had millions invested then I would wait it out and hope to get the full amount later," he said. "I invested just $500 and have no choice. I'm desperate."
